title: Where to See Autumn Leaves in Korea: 6 Best Fall Foliage Spots for October–November 2026
html:
Autumn is many Koreans' favorite season, and for good reason. From mid-October to early November, the mountains turn red, orange, and gold, the air is cool and dry, and the sky is almost always blue. Koreans even have a word for going out to see the colors: danpung (단풍, "autumn leaves") trips.

This guide picks 6 easy-to-reach autumn leaf spots for first-time visitors — three inside Seoul and three day or overnight trips — listed in the order their colors peak, so you can match them to your travel dates.

When Do the Leaves Change in 2026?

Leaves change from north to south and from high mountains down to the cities. So the colors start in the mountains of Gangwon-do (the province east of Seoul) and finish in the southern parts of the country and in Seoul's city streets.

The Korea Forest Service (the government office that looks after Korea's forests) released its 2026 forecast in September. It says Seoraksan peaks around October 20, Songnisan around October 28, and Naejangsan around November 4. Across the country, maple trees should peak around October 31 and ginkgo trees (the trees with fan-shaped leaves that turn bright yellow) around October 30.

"Peak" here means about half of the leaves have changed color. The colors usually stay beautiful for about 1–2 weeks around that date, so you don't have to hit the exact day. Weather can shift things by a few days, so check the latest news a week before you go.

1. Seoraksan National Park (Sokcho) — Peak: Around October 20

Seoraksan (설악산, "Seorak Mountain") is the first famous mountain in Korea to turn red each year, and many Koreans think it's the most beautiful. It sits near the east coast city of Sokcho (속초), so you can combine mountain leaves with the sea in one trip.

You don't have to be a hiker. From the main entrance (called Seorak-dong), there's a flat, easy path to Sinheungsa (신흥사), a Buddhist temple surrounded by maples. If you want a view from above without climbing, take the Seoraksan Cable Car to Gwongeumseong, a rocky peak with wide views. A round trip was about ₩16,000 for adults at the time of writing.

Getting there: Take an express bus from Dong Seoul Bus Terminal or Seoul Express Bus Terminal to Sokcho (about 2.5 hours), then a city bus (No. 7 or 7-1) or a taxi to the park entrance. Entry to the national park itself is free.

Tip: Peak weekends are extremely busy, and the cable car line can take over an hour. Go on a weekday and arrive early in the morning. Since Sokcho is far from Seoul, staying one night makes the trip much more relaxed.

2. Nami Island (Gapyeong) — Peak: Late October to Early November

Nami Island (남이섬, Namiseom) is a small island in a river about 1 hour from Seoul. It became famous worldwide from the Korean drama Winter Sonata, and today it's one of the most popular day trips for foreign visitors. In autumn, its long rows of ginkgo and maple trees turn the whole island yellow and red.

Getting there: Take the ITX-Cheongchun train (a fast commuter train) from Yongsan Station or Cheongnyangni Station to Gapyeong Station (about 1 hour). From Gapyeong Station, a taxi or local bus to the ferry pier takes about 10 minutes. The short ferry ride to the island is included in your ticket.

Ticket: About ₩19,000 for adults, including the round-trip ferry. Nami Island calls itself a "republic" for fun, so your ticket is called a "visa" — don't worry, it's just a ticket. The island stays open later in fall foliage season.

3. Haneul Park (Seoul) — Silver Grass Festival: October 17–23

Not every autumn color comes from trees. Haneul Park (하늘공원, "Sky Park") is a hilltop park in western Seoul covered with eulsae (억새, silver grass) — tall, feathery grass that turns silver and gold in October and glows at sunset. Fun fact: this hill used to be a giant garbage landfill. It was turned into a park for the 2002 World Cup.

The 25th Seoul Silver Grass Festival runs from October 17 to 23, 2026 (10:00–21:00), with evening lights in the grass field. Entry is free.

Getting there: Take Line 6 to World Cup Stadium Station and walk about 20 minutes to the park entrance. Then either climb the wooden staircase (about 290 steps, around 15 minutes) or take the small electric shuttle (called Maengkkongi, "little frog") from the parking lot below. The hill is very crowded during the festival, so public transport is much easier than a car.

4. Changdeokgung Palace and Its Secret Garden (Seoul) — Peak: Late October to Early November

Changdeokgung (창덕궁) is a royal palace from the Joseon dynasty (Korea's last kingdom, 1392–1910) and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Behind it is the Huwon (후원), or Secret Garden — a quiet royal garden with ponds, wooden pavilions, and old trees. Many Koreans say it's the single best place in Seoul to see autumn colors.

Important: The Secret Garden needs a separate ticket from the main palace, and the number of visitors is limited. In autumn, tickets often sell out, so book online in advance on the official palace ticket website if you can. Some tickets are also sold at the gate on the day, but they go fast. At the time of writing, palace entry was ₩3,000 and the Secret Garden added about ₩5,000 — check the official site before you go, as fees may change.

Getting there: Anguk Station (Line 3), Exit 3, then about a 5-minute walk. Closed on Mondays.

5. Deoksugung Stone Wall Road (Seoul) — Peak: Late October to Early November

If you only have an hour, go here. Deoksugung Doldam-gil (덕수궁 돌담길, "Deoksugung Stone Wall Road") is a walking street along the old stone wall of Deoksugung Palace, right in the middle of the city. In autumn, the ginkgo trees along the wall turn bright yellow, and the fallen leaves make the street look like a golden carpet.

It's free and open 24 hours. At night the wall is lit up, which is a lovely (and less crowded) time for a walk. Nearby you'll find the Seoul Museum of Art and many small cafés along Jeongdong-gil street.

Getting there: City Hall Station (Line 1 or 2) — follow the signs for Deoksugung. The palace's main gate, Daehanmun, is right by the station exit, and the wall road starts just to its left.

Heads up: Ginkgo trees drop small round seeds in autumn that smell quite bad when stepped on. It's harmless — just watch where you step!

6. Naejangsan National Park (Jeongeup) — Peak: Around November 4

If you're visiting in early November and the northern mountains are already past their best, head south to Naejangsan (내장산, "Naejang Mountain"). Many Koreans call it the best autumn leaf mountain in the whole country. It's famous for its small maple leaves that turn a very deep red, and for a long tunnel of maple trees on the road to Naejangsa (내장사), a Buddhist temple inside the park.

The most famous photo spot is Uhwajeong (우화정), a small pavilion on a pond that reflects the red mountains like a mirror. There's also a cable car if you'd like a view from above without hiking.

Getting there: Take the KTX or SRT (Korea's high-speed trains) from Yongsan Station or Suseo Station to Jeongeup Station (about 1.5–2 hours). From there, take city bus No. 171 or a taxi (about 20 minutes) to the park. The bus doesn't come often, so a taxi is easier. Entry to the park is free.

Photo: Tung Thanh Dang, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Tip: Naejangsan gets very crowded on peak weekends, and the roads near the park can be jammed for hours. A weekday visit by train is by far the easiest way.

How Koreans Actually Go Leaf-Peeping

Autumn leaf trips are a big deal in Korea, so a few local habits will help you plan:

  • Koreans dress for hiking — even on easy paths. You'll see colorful hiking jackets everywhere. You don't need special gear for the spots in this guide, but comfortable shoes and a light jacket are a must. Mornings in the mountains can be close to 0°C in late October.
  • Locals go early and on weekdays. Many Koreans leave Seoul before 7 a.m. on peak weekends to beat the traffic. If your schedule is flexible, a weekday is the single best way to avoid crowds.
  • Locals check the "danpung" news. Korean news and weather sites post daily updates on how much each mountain has changed. Search "단풍 현황" (autumn leaf status) plus the mountain name — the photos will tell you a lot even if you can't read Korean.
  • Tour buses are popular, too. For far-away spots like Seoraksan and Naejangsan, many travelers (Korean and foreign) join a one-day bus tour from Seoul. It's a long day, but you don't have to deal with transfers.

meta_description: Where to see autumn leaves in Korea in 2026: 6 easy fall foliage spots, peak dates, how to get there from Seoul, and tips.
